title: Why it was written down
hookLine: after the revolts against Rome, the oral teachings risked being lost

lines: TURN LEFT AT THE DEAD OAK.
cards: Directions to a good fishing spot, the way an old neighbor gives them. Drive past the church. Turn left at the dead oak.
Park where the fence leans, and walk toward the sound of the water. Perfect directions, as long as the oak stands.
Then a storm takes the oak, a new owner fixes the fence, and the only person who knew the way moves to another state. The directions haven't changed. The landmarks have.
The oral Torah lived like that, in teachers and the places they taught. Then came the wars with Rome.

teach.h: A TEACHING THAT LIVES IN PEOPLE.
teach.b: Why it was written down. The oral teaching was meant to live in mouths: a teacher says it, a student says it back.

teach.h: THE WARS WITH ROME; THE LANDMARKS FALL.
teach.b: But after the Temple fell and the revolts against Rome were crushed, Jewish tradition remembers teachers killed and houses of study broken up. A teaching that lives only in people can die with them.
So, tradition says, Rabbi Judah the Prince gathered it into the Mishnah. Here's the surprise. The Mishnah isn't a roomy book that explains itself.

teach.h: TERSE, TIGHT, MADE TO BE MEMORIZED.
teach.b: It's terse. It loves lists and patterns. One chapter of Pirkei Avot runs on numbers: with ten sayings the world was created; ten generations from Adam to Noah.
That's how you write something people will learn by heart. It was written down so it could go back into the mouth. The idea is older than the Mishnah.

teach.h: WRITE THE SONG; PUT IT IN THEIR MOUTHS.
teach.b: Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses is told to write down a song, and in the same breath to teach it to the people and put it in their mouths.
Written, so it won't be lost. Spoken, so it stays alive. The Torah itself warns, in Hebrew, pen tishkach: lest you forget the things your eyes have seen.
A song of hope, Hatikvah; from generation to generation; the Torah on the mouth: lately this path keeps circling one worry. How do you keep something alive after the people who knew it are gone?

how: Jews study the Mishnah by reading it aloud, often with a study partner, and some learn passages by heart; there are groups that study a portion of the Mishnah each day.

games.q: you're a teacher after the wars with Rome. your teachers are gone and your students are scattered. the teaching lives only in memory. what do you do?
o: keep it spoken only, and hope enough people remember.
write a huge book that explains every reason.
gather it into a terse text people can still learn by heart.
games.why: tradition says Rabbi Judah the Prince gathered it into the Mishnah: written so it wouldn't be lost, terse enough to stay on the mouth.

practice: Let one thing come to mind that lives nowhere but in your memory: a grandparent's saying, the way to a place, a song someone used to sing you. Stay with its details, the voice, the room, the order things happened.
Then shape it into a few short, plain lines, the way the Mishnah would, so someone else could learn it by heart.

wordCard.voice: Why it was written down. After the wars with Rome, a spoken teaching that could have died with its teachers was set down in the Mishnah, terse enough to memorize. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: lest you forget, the Torah's warning in Deuteronomy.

carryVoice: Your line: write it before it's lost. Tomorrow, the teachers whose names fill the Mishnah. Until tomorrow.
